rows.question: How do I change the address on my driving licence?
keyFacts: It does not cost anything to change your address with DVLA
You can apply online (or by post)

answer.answer:
You can change the address on a full or provisional GB driving licence online through GOV.UK, for free. You'll need to sign in to your GOV.UK account (creating one if needed) and may be asked to prove your identity, usually with photo ID such as a passport. Online applications usually arrive within a week. You can keep driving while you wait for the new licence.

If you prefer, you can apply by post. For a photocard licence, fill in the 'changes' section of letter D741 (or use form D1 for cars/motorcycles or D2 for lorries/buses if you don't have the D741), and send it with your licence to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BN, with the correct postage. For a paper licence, send a completed D1 or D2, your licence, original identity documents and a passport photo. Postal applications usually take up to 3 weeks.

You must also update your vehicle log book (V5C) and your vehicle tax Direct Debit if you pay that way, and change the address on any personalised registration document (V750 or V778). Failing to tell DVLA about an address change can lead to a fine of up to £1,000. If you're moving abroad, you can't register the new address on a British licence; contact the licensing authority in your new country instead. Adding a new photo at the same time costs £14 online (no fee if you're over 70 or have a medical short-period licence).

rows.question: How long do penalty points stay on my licence?
keyFacts: Penalty points/endorsements stay on your driving record for 4 or 11 years, depending on the offence

answer.answer: It depends on the offence. Most penalty points (endorsements) stay on your driving record for 4 years, counted from the date of the offence (or from the date of conviction for some offences, such as reckless/dangerous driving or offences that result in disqualification). Certain offences, such as drink or drug driving (codes DR10–DR61) and causing death by careless driving while under the influence (CD40–CD60, CD70), stay for 11 years from the date of conviction. Codes DR40–DR70 (e.g. in charge of a vehicle over the limit) stay 4 years from the offence date, or from conviction where disqualification is imposed. The endorsement is 'valid' for the first 3 years (4-year endorsement) or 10 years (11-year endorsement) – a court can take it into account for a new offence during that time. Insurers and employers may see it for the first 4 years (4-year endorsement) or first 5 years (11-year endorsement, or first 30 months if under 18). Check your exact points and removal dates on your driving licence record.

rows.question: How do I tell DVLA my car is off the road?
keyFacts: Tell DVLA online (or by phone/post) that the vehicle is off the road: a SORN
You get a refund for any full months of remaining tax

answer.answer:
You tell DVLA by making a SORN (Statutory Off Road Notification), which registers the vehicle as off the road. Options:
- Online: if the vehicle is registered in your name, use the 11-digit number from the log book (V5C) or the 16-digit reference on your vehicle tax reminder (V11 letter, email or text).
- By phone: DVLA vehicle service, 0300 123 4321 (24-hour service).
- By post: send form V890 to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1AR. If the vehicle isn't registered in your name, fill in the relevant part of the log book and send it with the V890. If you have no log book, send a V62 (£25) with the V890.

Timing: the SORN starts immediately if your vehicle tax has already expired or you're not applying in the month your tax is due to expire. If you apply in the tax expiry month, it starts on the first day of the next month. You'll get a refund for any full months of remaining tax, and you can't use the vehicle on the road until you tax it again. If you've sold the vehicle, you don't need a SORN; tell DVLA you've sold it instead.

rows.question: Can I get a refund on my vehicle tax if I sell my car?
keyFacts: You cancel vehicle tax by telling DVLA you no longer have the vehicle (for example sold, scrapped or off the road); there is no other way
You get a refund for any full months of remaining tax

answer.answer: Yes. If you sell your car, tell DVLA that it has been sold or transferred (this is the only way to cancel vehicle tax). Direct Debits are cancelled automatically. You won't get back credit card fees, the 5% surcharge on some Direct Debit payments, or the 10% surcharge on a single 6-month payment. If the cheque hasn't arrived after 8 weeks, contact DVLA; if it's in the wrong name, return it to DVLA and tell them the correct name.

rows.question: Which vehicles are exempt from vehicle tax?
keyFacts: Historic vehicles built before 1 January 1986 are exempt from vehicle tax
Vehicles used by a disabled person can be exempt
Electric cars are no longer exempt: from 1 April 2025 they must pay vehicle tax

answer.answer:
Vehicles exempt from vehicle tax include:
- Vehicles used by a disabled person (claimed when applying for tax; only one vehicle at a time can use the exemption)
- Disabled passenger vehicles: vehicles (apart from ambulances) used by organisations providing transport for disabled people
- Historic vehicles: those made before 1 January 1986
- Mobility vehicles and powered wheelchairs: max speed 8mph on the road and fitted with a device limiting them to 4mph on footways
- Electric vehicles: only heavy goods vehicles over 3,500kg remain exempt from 1 April 2025 (electric cars, vans, motorcycles and tricycles now pay; hybrid electric vehicles must also pay)
- Mowing machines designed and used only for cutting grass (not tractors towing gang mowers)
- Steam-powered vehicles
- Agricultural, horticultural and forestry vehicles: tractors, agricultural engines, light agricultural vehicles used off-road, and 'limited use' vehicles making journeys of no more than 1.5km on a public road between land used by the same person

Also, if a vehicle is registered as off the road (SORN), you can get a refund for unused vehicle tax already paid. Note that you must still tax your vehicle even if you do not have to pay.

rows.question: How do I check the MOT history of a car?

It shows past MOT results: pass or fail, the mileage recorded at each test, and when the next MOT is due. For cars, motorcycles and vans, results are available only for tests since 2005.

To check that an MOT certificate is genuine, compare it against the MOT history.

rows.question: What do I need to do when I sell my car?
keyFacts: Tell DVLA you've sold or transferred the vehicle
You get a refund for any full months of vehicle tax left

answer.answer:
When you sell a car, you need to tell DVLA that you no longer own it:

1. Tell DVLA online (the "sold, transferred or bought a vehicle" service, open Mon–Fri 7am–9pm and Sat–Sun 7am–8pm). This changes the registered keeper and lets you send the log book (V5C) to the new keeper. You can't use the online service if you've already posted the V5C to DVLA, or if you don't have the log book.
2. If you don't have the log book, write to DVLA (Swansea, SA99 1BA) with: your name and address, the vehicle registration number, the make and model, the exact date of sale, and the name and address of the new keeper or motor trader. Make sure you pay the correct postage.
3. Give the new keeper the V5C log book. If you are selling to a motor trader, they fill in the yellow "sell, transfer or part-exchange your vehicle to the motor trade" section and you send the perforated section to DVLA.
4. Tell the buyer they need to apply for a new V5C using form V62 (£25 fee) if they don't receive a log book.
5. Your vehicle tax is cancelled once you tell DVLA, and you get a refund for any full months of tax remaining.

The buyer must tax the car before driving it (tax doesn't transfer), or declare it off the road with a SORN. The pages I checked don't cover insurance or number plate arrangements, so check those separately.

rows.question: How do I change the address on my V5C log book?
keyFacts: You can change the address online as the registered keeper, or by post
It is usually free to update your V5C

answer.answer:
You can change your V5C address online or by post. It's usually free.

Online: Go to the GOV.UK "Change your address on your vehicle log book" service (you must be the registered keeper). It's available Mon–Fri 7am–9pm and Sat–Sun 7am–8pm. You'll need your vehicle's registration number, your log book reference number and a UK address. It only works for a UK address.

By post:
- New-style log book (multi-coloured numbered blocks on the front): write the new address in section 3 (no PO Box), and send the whole log book to the DVLA address in section 3.
- Older-style log book: write the new address in section 6 (no PO Box), sign and send the whole log book to the DVLA address in section 8. Don't tick the 'new keeper' box or fill in your name on this form.
- Pay the correct postage.

Before you start: if the vehicle needs taxing within the next 4 weeks, tax it online using your current V5C first, or take the log book to a Post Office that deals with vehicle tax (take your MOT certificate if needed).

Also note: you must update your driving licence address and vehicle tax Direct Debit (if you pay that way), and you can be fined up to £1,000 if you don't tell DVLA. You can't use this service if you've already sent your log book to DVLA, have lost your log book (apply for a new one instead), have sold/bought the vehicle, or are moving abroad. If you're changing your name too, you must do it by post.

rows.question: What should I do if my car has been stolen?
keyFacts: Tell the police (dial 101) and your insurance company straight away
If the insurer pays out, you must tell DVLA the vehicle has been sold to the insurer

answer.answer:
1. Report it to the police straight away. Call 101 and ask for your local police. Have the registration number, make, model and colour ready. You'll get a crime reference number, which you need for your insurance claim. The police tell DVLA about the theft, and they also tell DVLA if the vehicle is found.
2. Call your insurance company straight away, give them the crime reference number, and ask how to make a claim.
3. If your insurer pays out, you must tell DVLA the vehicle has been sold to the insurance company. You can do this online or by sending the perforated section of the log book (yellow 'sell, transfer or part-exchange to the motor trade' section) to DVLA, with a letter giving the date the payment was accepted and your insurer's details. Give the rest of the log book to your insurer. If the insurer asks for the whole log book, write to DVLA (Swansea SA99 1BD) with your insurer's details, claim date, registration number, make, model, colour and your signature.
4. If you have a private (personalised) registration number you want to keep, apply to keep it as soon as the vehicle is stolen. You must apply within 2 years and 6 months of telling DVLA. You can only get it back if you told the police, and the vehicle had a valid MOT and up-to-date vehicle tax when stolen. You must get the number back before telling DVLA you no longer own the vehicle.

rows.question: What are the penalties for speeding?
keyFacts: The minimum penalty is a £100 fine and 3 penalty points
You could be disqualified if you reach 12 or more points within 3 years

answer.answer:
The minimum penalty for speeding is a £100 fine and 3 penalty points on your licence. 

- If you plead guilty to a Fixed Penalty Notice, you pay the £100 fine and get 3 points, unless you're offered and take a speed awareness course. You can usually take one only if the police consider it appropriate and you have not been on one in the past 3 years. The speeding code stays on your licence for 4 years.
- If you plead not guilty, the case goes to court. The court can fine you more and give you more points. The fine is usually a percentage of your weekly income, up to a maximum of £1,000 (£2,500 for motorway speeding). You could also be disqualified or have your licence suspended.
- Accumulating 12 or more penalty points within 3 years can lead to disqualification from driving.
- Endorsement codes for speed limit offences carry 3 to 6 penalty points depending on the offence (e.g. SP30 for exceeding a public road limit, SP50 for a motorway limit). These codes stay on your driving record for 4 years from the offence date.

rows.question: How do I get my licence back after a driving ban?
keyFacts: You must apply for a new licence to drive again
For drink or drug driving you can reapply before the disqualification ends, using the D27 form DVLA sends

answer.answer:
Check when your ban ends first: go online to check your driving record, or wait for the reminder form D27 that DVLA sends 56 days before the end (90 days for some drink-drive or high-risk offenders, via a D27PH letter). Then:

- If you were disqualified (or your licence was revoked), you must apply for a new licence to drive again. For a drink or drug driving disqualification, you can apply before the ban ends, but you cannot drive until it is over. Send the completed D27 renewal form with the fee to DVLA (or use form D1 for a car or motorcycle, D2 for a lorry or bus, from a Post Office if you don't receive the D27).
- If your licence was cancelled within 2 years of passing your test (new driver), or you were a provisional licence holder who had passed but not yet applied for a full licence, you must apply for a new provisional licence and retake both parts of the driving test. If the court told you to retake the test, you need a new provisional licence before you can drive again.
- If your licence was revoked and you're not a new driver, apply for a new one at any time using form D1 (sent with the fee to the address on the form).
- If you failed to hand your licence to the court, apply with form D1 or D2 and the fee.
- In Northern Ireland, contact the Driver and Vehicle Agency (DVA) instead. Non-GB licence holders: DVLA returns your licence when the disqualification ends.

You can drive again once the ban is over and, where required, you have passed the tests you need to take.

rows.question: Can I drive if I have diabetes?
keyFacts: You must tell DVLA if your insulin treatment lasts (or will last) over 3 months
You do not need to tell DVLA if the diabetes is treated by diet alone

answer.answer:
Yes, in many cases you can drive with diabetes, but whether you must tell DVLA depends on your treatment and the licence you hold.

Car or motorbike licence:
- Diet-controlled diabetes: you do not need to tell DVLA.
- Non-insulin medication (tablets or non-insulin injections), or diet plus medication: check with your doctor or nurse whether you need to tell DVLA. If you do, complete form DIAB1 and send it to DVLA.
- Insulin: you must tell DVLA if your insulin treatment lasts (or will last) over 3 months. This includes gestational diabetes where insulin continues more than 3 months after the birth. You can report online or use form DIAB1.
- You must also tell DVLA if you get disabling hypoglycaemia (low blood glucose), or a medical professional has told you that you are at risk of developing it.

Bus, coach or lorry licence (stricter rules):
- Diet-controlled diabetes: you do not need to tell DVLA.
- Tablets or non-insulin injections: you must tell DVLA. Use form VDIAB1SG for sulphonylurea or glinide tablets, or form VDIAB1GEN for other tablets or non-insulin injections.
- Insulin: you must stop driving and tell DVLA when you start insulin. DVLA will tell you when you can drive again. Use form VDIAB1I.

Failing to tell DVLA about a relevant medical condition can lead to a fine of up to £1,000, and you may be prosecuted if you are involved in an accident as a result. If you are unsure what medication you are on, check with your nurse or doctor.

rows.question: What are the eyesight rules for driving?
keyFacts: You must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away
Minimum visual acuity of decimal 0.5 (6/12) on the Snellen scale, with glasses or contact lenses if needed

answer.answer:
Standards for car drivers (per GOV.UK):
- You must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres away. You can wear glasses or contact lenses if you need them for driving, and you must wear them every time you drive if you need them to meet the standard.
- Visual acuity of at least decimal 0.5 (6/12) on the Snellen scale, using both eyes together, or in the seeing eye if you have sight in one eye only (with glasses or contact lenses if needed).
- An adequate field of vision. An optician can check this.
- You must tell DVLA about any eyesight problem affecting both eyes (or the only eye if you have one). Short sight, long sight and colour blindness don't need to be reported. You don't need to report short-sight surgery if you meet the standards afterwards.
- Practical driving test: you must correctly read a number plate on a parked vehicle at the start. If you can't, you fail and the test doesn't continue, and DVLA is told and your licence is revoked.
- If you choose an eyesight test from another optician, it must include an Esterman visual test. DVLA doesn't guarantee acceptance, and you pay for it yourself.

Lorry and bus drivers have stricter standards: at least 0.8 (6/7.5) in the better eye and at least 0.1 (6/60) in the other, with glasses up to +8 dioptres or contact lenses. They also need a horizontal visual field of at least 160 degrees, and must report any eyesight problem affecting either eye.

rows.question: How do I change the photo on my driving licence?
keyFacts: It costs £14 to change the photo online
You do this by renewing your licence (online, or by post for £17)

answer.answer:
You change the photo by renewing your full or provisional driving licence, which gives you a new licence.

Online: Sign in to the DVLA renewal service and upload a new photo or use your passport-type photo. It costs £14. You must be a resident of Great Britain (Northern Ireland has a separate service) and not be disqualified from driving. You may be asked to prove your identity, usually with photo ID such as a passport or driving licence.

By post: Get a 'D1 pack' of forms from a Post Office that deals with DVLA photocard renewal. Send the completed forms with a recent printed passport-type photo, your current photocard and paper counterpart (if lost, tick the relevant box on the D1 form), and a £17 cheque or postal order payable to DVLA. There's no fee if you're over 70 or have a medical short period licence. Send everything to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1DH, and pay the correct postage.

If you've also changed your name, you'll need to include identity documents too.

rows.question: What do the codes on my driving licence mean?
keyFacts: The codes on the back of the licence set conditions you must meet to drive
Examples: 01 eyesight correction (glasses or contact lenses); 78 automatic transmission only

answer.answer:
The codes on the back of a GB driving licence are restriction/entitlement conditions you must meet to drive. Examples:

Medical/vehicle adaptation codes:
- 01: glasses or contact lenses needed for eyesight
- 02: hearing or communication aid needed
- 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 / 31 / 32 / 33 / 35: modified transmission, clutch, braking, accelerator, pedals or control layouts
- 40 / 42 / 43: modified steering, rear-view mirrors or driving seat
- 44 (and 44(1)–44(12)): motorbike modifications (e.g. 44(5) adjusted manual transmission/clutch, 44(8) seat height allowing both feet on the ground)
- 45: motorbikes only with sidecar

Vehicle and entitlement restrictions:
- 78: automatic transmission only
- 79: only vehicles matching the specification in brackets on the licence
- 101: not for hire or reward
- 102: drawbar trailers only
- 103: subject to certificate of competence
- 105: vehicle not more than 5.5 metres long
- 106: automatic transmission only
- 107: not more than 8,250 kg
- 110: transporting persons with restricted mobility only
- 111 / 113: limited to 16 passenger seats (113 except automatics)
- 115: organ donor
- 118: start date is for earliest entitlement
- 96: vehicle and trailer where trailer is at least 750kg and combined weight is 3,500–4,250kg
- 97: not allowed to drive C1 vehicles that require a tachograph
- 122: valid on completion of Basic Moped Training Course

Administrative codes:
- 70: exchanged licence
- 71: duplicate licence

Some codes may differ in Northern Ireland. The full list is on the GOV.UK driving licence codes page.

Endorsement codes (e.g. LC20, MR49) are different: they are offence codes recording convictions and penalty points, not conditions on your licence.

rows.question: How do I swap my paper driving licence for a photocard?
keyFacts: You do not need to exchange a valid paper licence unless you change your address or name, want to do Driver CPC training, or it is damaged, lost or stolen
It is free if you changed your name or address and still have the paper licence
Otherwise a new photocard licence costs £20

answer.answer:
You only need to exchange a paper licence if you have changed your address or name, want to do Driver CPC training, or your licence is defaced, lost, stolen or destroyed. If none of these apply and your paper licence is still valid, you don't need to swap it.

If you do need to exchange it:
- Online: sign in to the DVLA "renew/exchange" service on GOV.UK. You must be a resident of Great Britain, not disqualified or prevented from driving, and meet the minimum eyesight requirement. You may be asked to prove your identity, usually with photo ID such as a passport or driving licence. Changing your address or name while keeping your paper licence is free; for a defaced, lost, stolen or destroyed licence, or any other reason, it costs £20 (paid by Mastercard, Visa, Electron or Delta).
- By post (required if you've changed your name): fill in form D1 (cars and motorbikes) or D2 (buses and lorries), available from most Post Offices. Include your original identity documents, a colour passport-type photo and the £20 fee if it applies (cheques or postal orders payable to DVLA, no cash). Send to DVLA, Swansea, SA99 1BU (cars and motorbikes) or SA99 1BR (buses and lorries).

DVLA aims to send the new licence within 3 weeks, though it may take longer if your medical or personal details need checking. You can drive while you wait if you meet the conditions set out in the guidance ("Can I drive while my application is with DVLA?").

rows.question: How do I change my driving test appointment?
keyFacts: You can change a car driving test only 2 times
You must change it yourself; your instructor is not allowed to

answer.answer:
You must change your driving test yourself, online. Your instructor cannot do it for you. The online service runs from 6am to 11:40pm (Northern Ireland has a separate service). You'll need to give DVSA at least 2 of: your driving licence number, your theory test pass certificate number, or your driving test booking reference.

You can find an earlier test (a cancellation appointment), move your test to a later date, or change the test centre to a nearby one. Changing the date, time or centre counts as one change, even if you change more than one thing at once. For a car driving test you can make 2 changes. If you need more after that, you must cancel and book a new test. You get a full refund if you cancel at least 10 full working days before the test date. Changes DVSA makes itself (for example, due to bad weather) don't count against your limit.

rows.question: How do I tax a car if I haven't received a tax reminder?
keyFacts: You can tax online with the 11-digit reference number from your V5C (or the 12-digit number on the green new keeper slip)
You can also tax by phone or at a Post Office

answer.answer:
You don't need the reminder letter (V11), email or text to tax your vehicle. You can tax it:

- Online: you need the 11-digit reference number from your V5C logbook (if you're the current keeper), or the 12-digit reference number from the green new keeper slip (if you've just bought the car and don't have a V5C in your name yet).
- By phone: call DVLA on 0300 123 4321 with your V5C or new keeper slip to hand.
- At a Post Office that deals with vehicle tax: take your V5C in your name (or a V62 application if you're the current keeper, or the new keeper slip), plus payment. Bring evidence of a current MOT (such as your MOT certificate or MOT history screenshot) if you have one. You can also set up a Direct Debit there, bringing your address, date of birth and bank details.

If you're in Northern Ireland, you also need an MOT certificate valid when the tax starts and an insurance certificate or cover note.

If you don't have a V5C or new keeper slip: current keepers must apply for a replacement V5C (£25) and can tax at the same time. New keepers can't tax without the new keeper slip and must apply for a new V5C by post.

You can check online that your vehicle has been taxed. Driving untaxed is illegal and can result in an £80 fine.

rows.question: I've just bought a used car. What do I need to do to tax it and get it registered in my name?
keyFacts: You must tax the vehicle before you can use it on the road
The seller usually registers a used vehicle for you, online or by post
You can tax it using the reference number from the green 'new keeper' slip

answer.answer:
Tax and registration steps for a used car:

1. Tax it before you drive it. Tax doesn't transfer to you when you buy the car. You can tax it online at GOV.UK using the green 'new keeper' slip from the log book (V5C). You can also use a V5C in your name or a recent DVLA reminder. You must tax it even if the vehicle is exempt. (Alternatively, declare it off the road with a SORN.)

2. Registration into your name:
- Usually the seller registers it to you, online or by post. Online, the seller registers it to you, fills in the green 'new keeper' slip and gives it to you, and destroys the old V5C. By post, the seller completes the V5C section for new keeper (section 2 on the new-style V5C, section 6 on the old style, plus the section 8 declaration on the old style), fills in the new keeper slip, and sends the V5C to DVLA.
- If the car has no V5C, don't buy it; DVLA advises against it. If you still go ahead, download form V62 and send it to DVLA with the £25 fee and the new keeper slip from the most recent V5C. If you already have a V5C but it hasn't been registered to you, you can also use form V62 to get a new one.
- If the V5C hasn't arrived 4 weeks after you sent in form V62, contact DVLA.

3. Check the V5C when it arrives. The details are your responsibility to check.

The pages didn't state a specific deadline for telling DVLA about the purchase, so check the GOV.UK 'Tell DVLA you've sold, transferred or bought a vehicle' page if you need one.

rows.question: I'm moving house. Which of my licence and vehicle records do I need to update?
keyFacts: Change the address on your driving licence
Change the address on your vehicle log book (V5C) and your vehicle tax Direct Debit, if you pay that way

answer.answer:
When you move house, update these records with DVLA:

1. Driving licence (full or provisional): change the address online or by post. It's free, and you can keep driving while you wait for the new licence. Postal applications usually take about 3 weeks to arrive. If you're also changing your name, you must apply by post.
2. Vehicle log book (V5C): change the address online for a UK address. rows.question: I'm over 70 and have a medical condition. How do I renew my driving licence?
keyFacts: You can renew online for free from 70 if you meet the eyesight requirement and nothing prevents you from driving
You must tell DVLA about medical conditions that affect your driving

answer.answer:
Renew at 70 the same way as anyone else, but declare your medical condition on the application. Check first that you're a Great Britain resident, meet the minimum eyesight requirement, and are not prevented from driving for any reason (C1/D1 entitlements must be renewed by post; Northern Ireland uses a different service).

Apply online at GOV.UK (sign in, possibly prove identity; free), or by post using the D46P form, which DVLA sends 90 days before your 70th birthday or licence expiry (otherwise use form D1 from a Post Office). Postal licences usually arrive in about 3 weeks, longer if medical details need checking.

If you have a notifiable condition, the application form asks for it; you don't need to contact DVLA separately. Failing to report a condition that could affect driving can bring a fine of up to £1,000.

DVLA may contact your doctor, arrange an examination, or ask for a driving or eyesight test. It can issue a shorter licence (1, 2, 3 or 5 years), require car adaptations, or tell you to stop driving.

You can keep driving while DVLA considers the application only if: your doctor supports you continuing; you had a valid licence; you drive only under the previous licence's conditions; the application is under a year old; your last licence wasn't revoked or refused for medical reasons; and you're not currently disqualified.

After 70, you must renew every 3 years.
